The Longnose anchovy (Anchoa nasus) reaches a maximum standard length of 17 cm [Li = 17 cm], a size that positions it among the larger members of its genus within the coastal pelagic fish community of the eastern Pacific. This species exhibits a relatively fast life history, with individuals attaining sexual maturity at a standard length of only 6 cm [Lp = 6 cm]. The pronounced difference between the size at puberty and the ultimate length indicates a substantial post-maturation growth phase, during which individuals continue to allocate resources to somatic development while simultaneously engaging in reproductive activity. This pattern is typical of many engraulids, which often face high natural mortality from predation during their early life stages. The ability to reproduce at a modest size may confer a demographic advantage in environments where adult survival is unpredictable, allowing a portion of the population to contribute offspring before encountering age-dependent sources of mortality.

At the onset of reproductive activity, an individual of the Longnose anchovy typically weighs approximately 1.42 grams [Wwp = approximately 1.42 grams], representing the wet weight at puberty derived from the length-mass relationship documented for this species. The disparity between this value and the ultimate wet weight of 37.5 grams [Wwi = 37.5 grams] underscores the considerable scope for growth that persists after the initiation of breeding. This post-pubertal mass increase is fueled by intense feeding on zooplankton, which supports both the energetic demands of gamete production and the continued expansion of body size. Field surveys along the coasts of Peru and northern Chile indicate that adult individuals commonly approach this asymptotic mass, with the largest specimens typically being gravid females. The length-mass allometry, consistent with the value of 3.14 employed in growth models for related clupeiforms, yields these widely accepted estimates for body size benchmarks in population assessments.

The egg diameter of the Longnose anchovy has been documented at 0.6 millimeters, a value that corresponds to an initial dry mass at birth of approximately 0.00011 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00011 grams]. This remarkably small birth mass, typical of pelagic-spawning engraulids, reflects the production of transparent, yolk-laden eggs that are released directly into the water column. The lecithotrophic phase following eclosion is brief, as the yolk-sac larva must develop functional feeding structures rapidly to avoid starvation in the planktonic environment. The chorionate embryo relies entirely on endogenous reserves during the first few days post-fertilization. At a sustained water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the interval from egg fertilization to the emergence of the yolk-sac larva is approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days]. This rapid developmental rate is consistent with observations in the congeneric European anchovy (Engraulis encrasicolus) under similar thermal regimes, suggesting a conserved physiological response to warm-water incubation.

Under the same thermal conditions of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum lifespan of the Longnose anchovy has been recorded at approximately 2.5 years [am = approximately 2.5 years], equivalent to about 912 days. This relatively short longevity is characteristic of small, fast-growing pelagic teleosts that experience high rates of natural mortality. The lifespan is tightly linked to the energetic demands of a warm-water existence, where elevated metabolic rates accelerate the pace of senescence. Comparative studies within the Engraulidae family show that species inhabiting cooler waters, such as the Argentine anchovy, often exhibit longer lifespans, underscoring the role of temperature in modulating life-history strategies. The 2.5-year maximum observed in Anchoa nasus aligns with the expectation for a species that invests heavily in early reproduction and rapid biomass turnover, a strategy well-suited to the productive but variable upwelling ecosystems of the Humboldt Current system.

Recent laboratory rearing experiments have further clarified the relationship between temperature and developmental milestones in the Longnose anchovy. At the standard reference condition of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the yolk-sac resorption and onset of first exogenous feeding occur rapidly after the 6-day incubation period (6 days) [ab = 6 days], allowing larvae to exploit the abundant microzooplankton in coastal waters. The low dry weight at birth of 0.00011 grams [Wwb = 0.00011 grams] necessitates a swift trophic transition to avoid the point of no return. Post-metamorphic juveniles grow quickly, recruiting into the adult population at a standard length of 6 cm [Lp = 6 cm] and a corresponding wet weight of 1.42 grams [Wwp = 1.42 grams]. The upper size limit of 17 cm [Li = 17 cm] in standard length is attained by the largest individuals, typically gravid females, and the maximum wet weight of 37.5 grams [Wwi = 37.5 grams] defines the upper bounds of somatic investment in this species. The species' maximum longevity, documented at 2.5 years [am = 2.5 years] under controlled conditions, reflects the accelerated pace of life characteristic of small pelagic teleosts in warm upwelling systems at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. These life-history traits, all measured under controlled thermal conditions, provide a robust framework for understanding the population dynamics of this important forage fish in its native habitat.
